As of 217 AM EDT Tuesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Strengthening deep southerly flow ahead of a 
developing low will support scattered to numerous showers and 
thunderstorms today, with locally heavy rainfall being the main
threat. Dewpoints in the 60s today will locally reach near 70 
over the Saint Lawrence Valley and portions of the Champlain 
Valley. This will translate to a slightly more humid air mass 
today, though temperatures will not be quite as warm as 
yesterday. Throughout the day today, a shortwave aloft will dig 
into the base of broader longwave troughing over eastern Canada,
eventually closing off into a closed low over the northeastern 
US later today. The approaching system has triggered the 
development of scattered showers and thunderstorms upstream, 
which will increase in coverage as they move eastward into our 
forecast area today. Minimal deep-layer shear will limit 
overall severe potential, and the greatest threat for today's 
thunderstorms will remain heavy downpours. It continues to 
appear that the most likely area to receive locally heavy 
rainfall today will be northern NY and southern Vermont, where 
today's rainfall amounts will range from 0.5 to 1.0+ inches. 
Higher resolution models indicate some isolated swaths of 1-2 
inches are possible today in these areas, especially if multiple
storms or heavy showers track over the same area. Central and 
northern Vermont will generally see rainfall amounts today under
0.5 inch, though some areas could see locally higher amounts if
a heavier storm moves over. These ranges are the general 
expected QPF amounts for today, but expect high variability in 
QPF swaths based on where individual storms track today.
Overall, these amounts could result in ponding in poor drainage
areas, but the overall flood risk for today is relatively low 
due to antecedent dry conditions. The exception would be if any
showers or thunderstorms continually train over the same area
and locally exceed flash flood guidance. For reference, current
one hour flash flood guidance from the NERFC is around 1.5-2.5
inch/hour, and current three hour flash flood guidance is 2-3
inch/hour. We will be watching hydro closely today, but
widespread issues are not anticipated.  

KEY MESSAGE 2:  Overnight tonight, showers and thunderstorms will 
continue as the low shifts closer. With warm cloud depths 
supporting efficient rainfall production and precipitable water 
values 1.5 to 1.75 inch, locally heavy rainfall remains a threat
overnight, though waning instability will temper overnight 
rainfall rates somewhat. The flow will increase from the 
southeast overnight, which will allow for some increased 
topographic influences in the overnight QPF forecast. This 
pattern favors higher overnight rainfall amounts over the 
eastern slopes of the southern Greens along with the eastern 
slopes of the Adirondacks. With the prolonged precipitation
event, the relative flood risk does increase slightly going into
Tuesday night, especially as noted before if multiple heavy
showers train over the same area. Widespread issues are not
anticipated, but isolated flash flooding can't be ruled out.  

Periods of rain, locally heavy at times, will continue through the 
day Wednesday and into Wednesday night.  By Wednesday morning, the 
surface low will be centered near northern New Jersey.  The system 
will send waves of rain northward through our forecast area, 
interspersed with some drier periods especially further north. 
Instability Wednesday will be lower than the previous few days, 
which will keep coverage of thunderstorms more limited.  This in 
turn will somewhat limit rainfall rates without the convective 
aspect, though the moist atmosphere and additional lift in 
orographically favored areas (mainly eastern slopes of the southern 
and central Greens along with eastern slopes of the Adirondacks) 
will maintain the localized heavy rain and isolated flash flood threat.
Rainfall totals for Wednesday and Wednesday night will be 
highest in these orographically favored areas, where 0.75-1.5 
inches are forecast. Elsewhere , rainfall amounts will range 
from 0.25 to 0.5 inch...lowest in rain shadowed areas of the 
Northeast Kingdom. 

The heavy rain threat and isolated flood threat comes to an end
Thursday as the low weakens and departs. Scattered showers will
weaken through the day and additional rainfall amounts will be 
limited to just a few additional tenths of an inch. 

KEY MESSAGE 3: An unsettled weather pattern will continue into the 
weekend as our approaching system slowly departs Friday with an 
additional system possibly arriving sometime late into the weekend.

approaching system and the weekend system, but trends have moved
